summary: Describes an architecture for Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3), emulating services such as Frame Relay, ATM, Ethernet, TDM, and SONET/SDH over packet networks using IP or MPLS, and presents the framework for pseudo wires.

plainLanguage.summary: An old leased line or Frame Relay circuit is a private wire between two sites. This document describes how to carry that same service across a shared packet network so the customer never notices the difference. Bits go in one side, cross the network in packages, and come out the other side looking like the original wire.

questions: how does a pseudo wire work over mpls
subtitle: How a packet network pretends to be a plain wire, so older services like leased lines and Frame Relay keep working unchanged.

tldr.problem: Providers wanted to replace old time division and frame based links with a shared IP or MPLS network, but customers still need the service to look and behave exactly like the wire it replaces.
tldr.mechanism: Two provider edge devices encapsulate the customer's native bits, cells or packets and carry them over a tunnel through the packet network, replaying them faithfully at the far side.
tldr.outcome: The PWE3 architecture let many legacy services ride over a modern packet core; RFC 3985 is Informational and was updated by RFC 5462.

sections.title: What PWE3 Does
sections.content:
Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge, or PWE3, emulates the essential attributes of a telecommunications service, such as a T1 leased line or a Frame Relay circuit, over a packet switched network. It aims to provide only the minimum functionality needed to reproduce the wire faithfully for a given service. Switching is the job of a forwarder function, and any translation that needs to understand the payload is the job of native service processing; neither is defined by PWE3 itself.

A pseudo wire encapsulates the service specific bit streams, cells or packets arriving at an ingress port and carries them across an IP path or MPLS tunnel, sometimes also managing timing and order so the service behaves as expected. From the customer edge equipment's point of view, the pseudo wire looks like an unshared link or circuit of the chosen service. Where the emulation falls short, those limitations must be described in the service specific documents.

For each service there is one default mode that every offering provider edge must support, with optional modes allowed when their extra complexity is clearly worth the improved faithfulness. The document deliberately does not define the on the wire encapsulation formats or the detailed setup and maintenance protocols; those live in other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: PWE3 makes a packet network act like a physical wire for one customer's service. It does the smallest job that keeps the service working, and leaves switching and translation to other parts of the provider equipment.

sections.title: The Reference Model
sections.content:
In the reference model, two provider edge devices provide one or more pseudo wires on behalf of the customer edge devices at each end. An attachment circuit connects each customer edge to its provider edge. A PSN tunnel is set up to give the pseudo wire a data path across the packet switched network. The pseudo wire traffic is invisible to the core network, and the core is transparent to the customer edges.

Native data units arrive over the attachment circuit, are encapsulated into a pseudo wire PDU, and cross the network inside the tunnel. The provider edges encapsulate and decapsulate the traffic and handle functions such as sequencing or timing. A pseudo wire demultiplexer value identifies a pseudo wire in the data plane; it must be unique per tunnel endpoint, which is what lets many pseudo wires share one tunnel.

The architecture is described as a stack of layers: the payload, the encapsulation layer, the pseudo wire demultiplexer, an optional PSN convergence layer, then the PSN, data link and physical layers. The encapsulation layer carries whatever extra information the far side needs and may be empty. The PSN convergence layer adapts the PSN so the pseudo wire sees a consistent interface, making pseudo wires independent of the PSN type; when the PSN already meets the requirements, it too is empty.
sections.plainLanguage: Two provider routers sit at the edges, one near each customer site. Each customer connects to its local router by a normal circuit, and the two routers carry the customer's traffic through a shared tunnel in the middle.

sections.title: Payload Types and Minimum Intervention
sections.content:
The payload is one of four generic kinds of native data unit: a packet, a cell, a bit stream, or a structured bit stream. Packets cover Ethernet, HDLC framing, Frame Relay and ATM AAL5 PDUs. Cells cover ATM. Unstructured bit streams cover E1, T1, E3 and T3. Structured bit streams cover SONET and SDH, for example the synchronous payload envelope or a set of DS0 channels. Each kind has its own handling for boundaries, sequencing, timing and possible fragmentation.

A packet payload is a variable size unit, normally relayed across the pseudo wire as one piece, but it may need fragmentation when it is larger than the PSN path MTU. A cell payload replays fixed size groups of octets, and several cells may be concatenated into one payload to save per packet overhead, trading a little delay and loss sensitivity for efficiency. A bit stream replays the pattern on the wire without using any internal structure, while a structured bit stream uses knowledge of that structure, which allows parts of the original stream, such as SONET section and line overhead, to be stripped and restored.

Guiding all of this is the principle of minimum intervention: the payload should be transported as received, with as few changes as possible. That keeps payload development separate from pseudo wire development and avoids unwanted side effects from misrepresenting the payload. An intervening approach can be more efficient on the wire, but the intermediate format becomes a new framing type that needs its own documentation and interoperability guarantees.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers send four broad kinds of data: packets, fixed cells, raw bit streams, and structured bit streams. The best rule is to change the customer's data as little as possible, so that no subtle mistake creeps in.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Sequencing and Timing
sections.content:
The encapsulation layer adapts the specific payload type to the pseudo wire demultiplexer that carries it. It has three sub-layers: payload convergence, timing, and sequencing. Payload convergence is tailored to the payload type and carries the per packet information needed to replay the native data at the far interface. Timing and sequencing are generic and are used only when a payload type needs them, which lets their headers be omitted to save processing and bandwidth.

Sequencing provides three services: frame ordering, detection of duplicated frames, and detection of lost frames. These let the pseudo wire imitate the invariant properties of a physical wire. When packets arrive out of order, the receiver either drops the misordered ones or sorts them back into order; the choice depends on how badly loss hurts, the speeds involved, the delay that reordering adds, and how often misordering happens. The sequence number space may need to exceed 2^16 to avoid wrapping during a long disturbance. Timing covers clock recovery, which extracts transmission bit timing from the delivered packet stream, and timed delivery, which releases packets with a constant phase relative to the input.

Fragmentation is needed when a payload plus all its headers exceeds the path MTU. Because fragmentation is expensive, it should first be avoided by the equipment that originates the traffic; the point closest to the sender with fragmentation capability, normally the customer edge, should reduce the packet to fit. Only if that fails should the provider edge fragment, using a generic pseudo wire method or the PSN's own fragmentation. A provider edge is allowed not to support fragmentation, in which case it drops oversized packets and notifies management. Where a control word is used over MPLS, its flags, length and sequence fields carry much of what the other layers need in a compact form.
sections.plainLanguage: Each carried unit gets a small set of labels and a sequence number. The receiver uses the sequence number to put units back in order, spot duplicates and notice losses, and can also pace the flow so a real time service keeps its timing.

sections.title: PSN Requirements, Control and Management
sections.content:
PWE3 places three requirements on the layers that carry it across the PSN: multiplexing, fragmentation, and length and delivery. Multiplexing lets many pseudo wires share one tunnel, which saves resources. Where the underlying PSN cannot give the length of a pseudo wire PDU, the encapsulation layer must supply it. The service specific document must say whether a checksum is preserved across the pseudo wire or stripped and recalculated, a choice that trades work against bandwidth. Because the PSN can suffer congestion, providers must watch packet loss; if the carried traffic is not known to be friendly to other traffic, they should rate limit it or shut down pseudo wires to keep loss acceptable.

A pseudo wire must be set up before a service can run and torn down afterwards. Setup can be triggered by an operator, by the management plane, by attachment circuit signaling, or by auto discovery, and the provider edges exchange capabilities and a PW-TYPE identifier so each side can check that the attachment circuits are compatible. Where the native service has status, keep alive or control messages of its own, the emulated service must carry or reproduce them, and a group identifier can let one notification cover many circuits that fail together.

For management, the provider edge reports interface status and counts such as pseudo wire PDUs sent and received with and without errors, lost sequenced PDUs, service PDUs, and one way delay and delay variation. These counters belong in a pseudo wire specific MIB and should not duplicate existing ones. A layered set of MIBs ties the native service modules to the generic pseudo wire module and then to the PSN modules. Connection verification and traceroute are supported too, though because a pseudo wire is opaque to the customer, that information stays inside the provider's network.
sections.plainLanguage: Before traffic flows, the two ends must agree on what service they are carrying. While it runs, the provider keeps counters and checks the circuit is alive, so problems can be found without the customer seeing inside the network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PWE3 provides no means of protecting the integrity, confidentiality or delivery of the native data units, so using it can expose an environment to new threats. Assumptions that hold when all systems are joined by a point to point or circuit switched network may no longer hold when they are joined by an emulated wire over a packet network. The document does not attempt a full risk analysis, because the risks depend on the PSN.

An example makes the concern concrete. Some IETF standards use relatively weak security when communicating nodes are expected to be on the same local area network, and the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol is one such case. Those weak mechanisms become a larger opening when an emulated Ethernet is carried over a pseudo wire, because the apparent local network is now spread across a provider's core.

Attacks from inside the PSN may target the pseudo wire tunnel endpoint to disrupt the demultiplexing and tunnel services. Limiting who may reach that endpoint to legitimate remote provider edge sources is one defense. Protection must also stop spoofed tunneled data: validating traffic addressed to the demultiplexer endpoint is essential, and security protocols such as IPsec may be used by the demultiplexer layer to authenticate and protect data between the endpoints. A pseudo wire may signal that it needs stronger protection, and the demultiplexer layer may define several protection profiles. IPsec can protect data between two provider edges, but it cannot give the native service the same guarantees it would have had on a real dedicated wire.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudo wire does not by itself keep the customer's data secret or untampered. Anything that was safe only because it never left a local network can become unsafe once it is carried across a provider's shared core, so the provider must limit who can reach the tunnel and can add encryption.

layers.detail: Payload convergence, timing and sequencing; may be empty.
